interest: This file provides a revealing perspective on U.S. pre-World War II intelligence gathering, national defense anxieties, and the legal-diplomatic complexities surrounding the Japanese diaspora in the Western Hemisphere. It highlights the acute American sensitivity toward Japanese consular registration of overseas nationals and second-generation Nisei (dual citizens), reflecting official fears of fifth-column activities and foreign conscription on American soil. Additionally, the collection captures inter-American intelligence sharing regarding Japanese hemispheric infiltration (specifically tracing Japanese nationals proficient in Spanish), offers detailed statistical data on the Japanese Empire's 1940 census published just prior to the outbreak of the Pacific War, and illustrates the lobbying and intelligence role played by anti-Japanese diaspora groups like Kilsoo K. Haan's Sino-Korean Peoples' League.
overview: This file (decimal file 894.5011) spans October 1940 through October 1941 and documents U.S. diplomatic, military, and naval surveillance of Japan's 1940 national census, with particular focus on its extension to overseas Japanese populations in the United States, the Territory of Hawaii, and Latin America. Prompted by concerns from the Governor of Hawaii, the Office of Naval Intelligence, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the War Department investigated Japanese consular efforts in Honolulu and New York to register Japanese residents and second-generation Americans of Japanese ancestry (Nisei dual citizens) for military and national defense purposes. The file includes translations of Japanese registration forms, demographic reports from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo detailing official imperial population statistics, U.S. diplomatic alerts to Latin American republics regarding a clandestine Japanese census of Spanish-speaking subjects, intelligence submissions from Korean nationalist Kilsoo K. Haan alleging extensive illegal entry networks, and military intelligence investigations into private census activities by Japanese nationals in Texas.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting a letter from the Department of the Interior regarding the Japanese census in Hawaii.
subfiles.from: Interior Department
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference sheet indexes an October 12, 1940 letter from the Department of the Interior (File No. 134 Hawaii/331). It records that the Governor of Hawaii forwarded a newspaper clipping reporting that American-born Japanese were being compelled by the Japanese consul in Honolulu to register for the census. The Governor requested that the State Department take action if the census violated international law.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Registration of American-born Japanese in Hawaii

subfiles.about: Letter from the Secretary of the Navy transmitting a naval intelligence report on the Japanese census in Hawaii.
subfiles.from: Frank Knox (Secretary of the Navy)
subfiles.summary: Secretary of the Navy Frank Knox transmits to Secretary of State Cordell Hull a report from the Commandant of the Fourteenth Naval District at Pearl Harbor regarding the Japanese census of overseas residents. Knox specifically draws Hull's attention to paragraphs 4 and 5 on page 2 of the enclosed report. The letter was received and routed through the Division of Communications and Records and the Division of Commercial Affairs.
subfiles.title: Letter from Secretary of the Navy Knox Transmitting Intelligence Report on Japanese Census

subfiles.about: Naval intelligence report translating Japanese census forms and regulations for overseas residents.
subfiles.from: Commander W. H. Hartt, Jr. and Rear Admiral C. C. Bloch (14th Naval District)
subfiles.summary: This multi-page intelligence report from the Fourteenth Naval District at Pearl Harbor provides an English translation of Japanese census questionnaires and instructions distributed via the Japanese Consulate and the United Japanese Society of Honolulu. It details the thirteen items of inquiry, which include family status, property holdings, education, foreign and Japanese language fluency, military service connections, and family registers. The report highlights rules governing dual citizens born before December 1, 1924, military exemptions, and fifty occupational categories.
subfiles.title: Intelligence Report: Census of Japanese Residents Abroad

subfiles.about: Letter transmitting an FBI photostat and translations of the Japanese census questionnaire distributed in the U.S. and Hawaii.
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover (Director, FBI)
subfiles.summary: FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover transmits to Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle, Jr. a photostatic copy of the questionnaire required for the Japanese 4th Census, along with two copies of an English translation of the Japanese instructions on the reverse. Hoover notes with concern that the questionnaire was distributed to second-generation Japanese in the United States and Hawaii. The letter was delivered by special messenger.
subfiles.title: Letter from J. Edgar Hoover to Adolf A. Berle, Jr. Regarding Japanese Census Questionnaire
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle, Jr. (Assistant Secretary of State)

subfiles.about: English translation of instructions issued by the Japanese Consulate in New York for the 4th Census.
subfiles.from: Imperial Japanese Consulate, New York (transmitted by FBI)
subfiles.summary: These pages provide duplicate copies of an English translation of the 'Caution concerning 4th Census' issued by the Imperial Japanese Consulate in New York. The text outlines four main points, emphasizing that overseas registration is a mandatory civic duty of Japanese citizens and serves as proof before foreign and Japanese officials. Crucially, item 4(c) instructs that second-generation nationals must register without fail.
subfiles.title: Consular Instructions: Caution Concerning 4th Census
subfiles.to: Japanese Residents in New York / U.S.

subfiles.about: State Department internal memorandum analyzing the Japanese census questionnaire and potential consular overreach.
subfiles.from: Frank A. Schuler, Jr. (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: The Division of Far Eastern Affairs analyzes the FBI transmittal, focusing on item 4(c) requiring second-generation persons to register. The memo questions whether Japanese consuls are soliciting persons of Japanese race who do not hold Japanese nationality, noting an estimated 46,000 such U.S. citizens in Hawaii. It recommends sending an inquiry to the FBI and, if substantiated, making diplomatic representations to the Japanese Embassy.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Japanese Consular Census Solicitation

subfiles.about: Inquiry from the State Department to the FBI regarding the registration of non-citizen Japanese Americans.
subfiles.from: Adolf A. Berle, Jr. (Assistant Secretary of State)
subfiles.summary: Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle, Jr. writes to FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover in follow-up to Hoover's December 2 letter. Berle requests clarification on whether available evidence indicates that Japanese consular census questionnaires are being distributed to American citizens of Japanese race who do not hold Japanese nationality.
subfiles.title: Letter from Adolf A. Berle, Jr. to J. Edgar Hoover Requesting Clarification on Census Target Population

subfiles.about: Letter transmitting a War Department Military Intelligence Division summary regarding Japanese registration of nationals.
subfiles.from: Brigadier General Sherman Miles (Acting Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2)
subfiles.summary: Brigadier General Sherman Miles, Acting Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, transmits to Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle, Jr. a confidential intelligence communication. The enclosed summary covers the Japanese registration of nationals in the United States for the State Department's information and appropriate action.
subfiles.title: War Department Transmittal Letter Regarding Japanese Registration of Nationals
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle, Jr. (Assistant Secretary of State)

subfiles.about: Military intelligence summary translating Japanese consular census instructions issued in New York.
subfiles.from: Military Intelligence Division (G-2), War Department
subfiles.summary: This confidential G-2 intelligence summary (G-2/1766-Z-629) provides the War Department's translation of instructions appended to the Japanese census registration blank from the Imperial Japanese Consulate in New York. The text reiterates the civic duty to register, assurances of confidentiality, submission requirements, and the explicit directive that second-generation nationals must register without fail.
subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Summary: Japanese Registration of Nationals
subfiles.to: War Department General Staff / State Department

subfiles.about: FBI reply clarifying that the Japanese census applied only to Japanese nationals and dual citizens.
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover (Director, FBI)
subfiles.summary: FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover replies to Assistant Secretary of State Berle's inquiry of December 26, 1940. Hoover clarifies that the Japanese census is directed at Japanese nationals and dual citizens. He confirms that there is no evidence indicating that the questionnaire was distributed by the Japanese government to American citizens of Japanese ancestry who do not possess Japanese nationality.
subfiles.title: Letter from J. Edgar Hoover to Adolf A. Berle, Jr. Clarifying Census Demographics
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle, Jr. (Assistant Secretary of State)

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch reporting published official results of the 1940 Census of the Japanese Empire.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew (U.S. Ambassador to Japan)
subfiles.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Japan Joseph C. Grew submits Despatch No. 5547 enclosing official population statistics from the national census of October 1, 1940, as published in the Official Gazette on April 18, 1941. The total population of Japan proper is reported as 73,114,308 and the Empire as 105,226,101, with comparative data going back to 1920. Grew notes that the domestic census enumerated military personnel as if they were at home and that results for Japanese residents abroad had not yet been released.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5547: The Population of Japan -- The 1940 Census

subfiles.about: Statistical table of the population of the Japanese Empire by constituent territories as of October 1, 1940.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Enclosure to Despatch No. 5547)
subfiles.summary: This confidential enclosure provides a breakdown of the population of the Japanese Empire by gender across its territorial components as of October 1, 1940. It lists population figures for Japan proper, Korea, Formosa, Japanese Saghalien, Kwantung Leased Territory, and the South Sea Islands under Japanese mandate, yielding an imperial grand total of 105,226,101 (52,896,862 males and 52,329,239 females).
subfiles.title: Statistical Enclosure 1: Population of Japanese Empire 1940 by Territory

subfiles.about: Statistical table detailing the population of Japan proper across all 47 prefectures in 1940.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Enclosure to Despatch No. 5547)
subfiles.summary: This enclosure lists the male, female, and total population of Japan proper by prefecture as of October 1, 1940. The enumeration spans all 47 administrative divisions, from Tokyo (7,354,971) and Osaka (4,792,966) down to smaller prefectures like Tottori (484,390) and Okinawa (574,579), concluding with Hokkaido (3,272,718).
subfiles.title: Statistical Enclosure 2: Population of Japanese Empire 1940 by Prefecture

subfiles.about: Statistical table tracking population growth between 1935 and 1940 in Japan's six largest cities.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Enclosure to Despatch No. 5547)
subfiles.summary: This statistical table provides comparative population data for Japan's six major cities between the 1935 and 1940 censuses. It details the total population, numerical increase, and percentage growth rate for Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka, Yokohama, Kobe, and Nagoya, highlighting significant expansion in Yokohama (37.5%), Nagoya (22.7%), and Tokyo (15.4%).
subfiles.title: Statistical Enclosure 3: Population in Six Major Cities in Japan

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting that Japan was taking a secret census of Japanese citizens fluent in Spanish.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew (U.S. Ambassador to Japan)
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports via Shanghai that his British diplomatic colleague in Tokyo telegraphed London that, according to a reliable informant, the Japanese government is conducting a census of all Japanese capable of reading and speaking Spanish. The substance of the telegram was communicated orally to the Office of Naval Intelligence and the Military Intelligence Division.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1144: Japanese Census of Spanish-Speaking Nationals

subfiles.about: Circular telegram alerting U.S. diplomatic missions in Latin America to the Japanese Spanish-language census.
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.summary: The Department of State dispatches a strictly confidential circular instruction to American diplomatic officers across the Latin American republics. Envoys are directed to inform their respective host Foreign Ministers confidentially that the U.S. government has learned from a reliable source that a census is being conducted in Japan of all Japanese citizens able to read and speak Spanish.
subfiles.title: Circular Telegram to American Diplomatic Officers in Other American Republics
subfiles.to: American Diplomatic Officers in Latin America

subfiles.about: Internal Department of State copy of Telegram 1144 with circular filing annotations.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew (U.S. Ambassador to Japan)
subfiles.summary: This document is an internal Department of State file copy of Ambassador Grew's Telegram No. 1144 of August 1, 1941, regarding the Spanish-speaking Japanese census. It bears administrative notations indicating that its contents were to be transmitted as a circular instruction to the chiefs of missions throughout the American republics.
subfiles.title: File Copy of Telegram No. 1144 with Routing Notations

subfiles.about: Telegram from Mexico City reporting the Mexican Foreign Minister's vigilance regarding Japanese activities.
subfiles.from: Josephus Daniels (U.S. Ambassador to Mexico)
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Josephus Daniels reports the reaction of Mexican Foreign Minister Ezequiel Padilla to the State Department's circular alert. The Foreign Minister welcomed the intelligence, affirmed that Mexico remains vigilant against any Japanese activities hostile to Western Hemisphere interests, and recalled that Mexico's response to a visiting Japanese mission had reaffirmed its commitment to continental solidarity over Japanese overtures.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 378 from Mexico City on Mexican Response to Japanese Census Alert

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting the delivery of the census warning to the Ecuadorian Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.from: Boaz Long (U.S. Minister to Ecuador)
subfiles.summary: U.S. Minister Boaz Long in Quito informs the Secretary of State that he communicated the contents of the Department's August 6 circular telegram to the Ecuadorian Minister for Foreign Affairs, who expressed his appreciation. Long observes that the comparatively few Japanese residents currently in Ecuador are known to acquire fluency in Spanish with ease.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1939: Notification to Ecuadorian Government Regarding Spanish-Speaking Japanese Census

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting delivery of the Spanish-language census alert to the Nicaraguan Foreign Minister.
subfiles.from: Pierre de L. Boal (U.S. Minister to Nicaragua)
subfiles.summary: U.S. Minister Pierre de L. Boal reports from Managua that he transmitted the confidential information regarding Japan's census of Spanish-speaking nationals to the Nicaraguan Minister for Foreign Affairs pursuant to the Department's circular telegram.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 16: Notification to Nicaraguan Foreign Minister Regarding Japanese Census

subfiles.about: Internal State Department note advising against acknowledging correspondence from the Sino-Korean Peoples' League.
subfiles.from: Vincent M. Anderson (Office of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: This handwritten internal note from the Office of Far Eastern Affairs advises against providing a written acknowledgment to Kilsoo K. Haan's communication. It notes the risk that any official receipt or reply from the Department could be utilized by Haan or his organization in an undesirable manner.
subfiles.title: Internal Memorandum on Sino-Korean Peoples' League Correspondence

subfiles.about: Letter from Korean nationalist Kilsoo K. Haan alleging Japanese census tracking of illegal entrants and dual citizens.
subfiles.from: Kilsoo K. Haan (Sino-Korean Peoples' League)
subfiles.summary: Kilsoo K. Haan, Washington Representative of the Sino-Korean Peoples' League, reports alleged Japanese Home Ministry figures showing 9,810 illegal Japanese entrants in the Western Hemisphere (including 2,810 in the U.S. and Hawaii, 545 in Canada, 817 in Mexico, and 5,638 in Latin America) and 159,565 dual citizens. Citing statements in the Tokyo Gazette and Honolulu's Nippu Jiji regarding total war mobilization and immunity for illegal entrants who register, Haan urges Secretary Hull to obtain consular census archives for national defense purposes.
subfiles.title: Letter from Kilsoo K. Haan Concerning Japanese Census, Illegal Entrants, and Dual Citizens

subfiles.about: Shanghai consular circular transmitting Japanese Consul-General Horiuchi's agreement to a local municipal census.
subfiles.from: Senior Consul, Shanghai / Tateki Horiuchi (Japanese Consul-General)
subfiles.summary: Circular No. 221-E-V from the Senior Consul of the Shanghai Consular Body circulates a letter from Japanese Consul-General Tateki Horiuchi. Horiuchi responds to a request from Mayor Chen Gongbo of the Japanese-backed municipal government regarding a census of foreign residents in the Western Shanghai area, confirming that he has instructed all Japanese residents in the district to comply promptly.
subfiles.title: Shanghai Consular Body Circular No. 221-E-V Regarding Western Shanghai Census

subfiles.about: War Department G-2 transmittal letter forwarding military intelligence summaries on Japanese activities.
subfiles.from: Brigadier General Sherman Miles (Acting Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2)
subfiles.summary: Brigadier General Sherman Miles of G-2 transmits four confidential intelligence communications to Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle, Jr. The listed enclosures cover a Communist Party communications article, a letter and MID summary concerning Kaname Andrew Susuki in Texas, and an intelligence report on Japanese immigrants in Ketchikan, Alaska.
subfiles.title: War Department Transmittal Letter with Intelligence Enclosures on Japanese Activities
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle, Jr. (Assistant Secretary of State)

subfiles.about: Military intelligence report investigating unauthorized Japanese census-taking by an alien in Orange, Texas.
subfiles.from: Headquarters Eighth Corps Area, Assistant Chief of Staff for Military Intelligence
subfiles.summary: This Eighth Corps Area intelligence summary reports that Kaname Andrew Susuki, a Japanese alien and long-time treasurer of the Orange Petroleum Company in Orange, Texas, had been privately conducting a census of Japanese residents. Susuki contacted postmasters across eight Texas counties to gather local Japanese names and addresses, prompting an investigation by the Immigration and Naturalization Service in Port Arthur seeking his deportation.
subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Summary: Reported Census of Japanese Conducted by K. A. Susuki in Texas
